quote: Just as "in the last days" the Word of God, clothed with flesh from Mary, came forth into this world, and one thing indeed was that which was seen in him, another that which was understood — for the appearance of the flesh in him lay open to all, but the recognition of his divinity was granted to few and to the elect —, so also, when through the prophets or the lawgiver the Word of God is brought forth to men, it is not brought forth without fitting garments. For as there it is covered by the veil of the flesh, so here by the veil of the letter, so that the letter indeed is looked upon as flesh, but the spiritual sense lying hidden within is perceived as divinity. Such, then, is what we now also find as we unroll the book of Leviticus, in which the rites of sacrifices and the diversity of victims and the ministries of the priests are described. But these things according to the letter,…

The beginning, then, of Leviticus says that "the Lord called Moses and spoke to him from the tabernacle of testimony," that he might promulgate to the sons of Israel the laws of sacrifices and of offerings, and it says: "If a man offer an offering to God, let him offer from the oxen or the flock," that is, lambs or kids; "but if from the birds, turtledoves or young of doves." "But if" not a man, but "a soul offer an offering to God, from fine flour," it says, "let him offer unleavened loaves baked in the oven, or indeed fine flour from the pan sprinkled with oil, or from the griddle likewise kneaded in oil." Then next we are taught that nothing "leavened" ought at all to be offered at the altar of God, nor should "honey" anywhere be mixed with the sacrifices, but every sacrifice or offering should be salted with "salt." In the second place he gave precept concerning the "sacrifices of…

And first I should like to see what this distinction is: that of one it says that "a man" offers, of another that "a soul" offers, of another "the high priest", of another "the synagogue", of another "one soul from the people of the land". And I think indeed that "a man" is to be understood as one who, made "to the image and likeness" of God, lives rationally. This man, then, offers to God an offering — a "bull-calf", when he has overcome the pride of the flesh; a "sheep", when he has corrected the irrational and foolish motions; a "kid", when he has conquered wantonness. He offers too "a pair of turtledoves", when he has not been alone, but has joined his mind to the Word of God as to a true spouse, just as this kind of bird is said to keep a single and chaste marriage. He offers too "two young pigeons", when he too has understood the mystery in which "the eyes of the bride" are said…

But if you wish to incline these things also to the moral level, you too have a "calf" which you ought to offer. Your flesh is a "calf," and indeed a very proud one; and if you wish to offer it as an offering to the Lord, so as to keep it chaste and modest, lead it "to the door of the tabernacle," that is, where it may be able to receive the hearing of the divine books. Let your offering be "male," let it not know woman, let it spurn concupiscence, let it flee frailty, let it seek nothing dissolute or soft. "Lay" also "your hand upon" your "victim," that it may be acceptable to the Lord, and slaughter it "before the Lord," that is, place upon it the bridle of continence, and do not take away from it the hand of discipline, just as that man laid his hand upon his own flesh who said: "I macerate my body and subject it to servitude, lest perhaps, when I have preached to others, I myself…

And yet: "he shall lay his hand," it says, "upon the head of the victim, and they shall slaughter the calf before the Lord, and the sons of Aaron the priest shall offer the blood, and they shall pour out the blood at the altar round about, which is at the door of the tabernacle of testimony." It can indeed seem to have been said for this reason, that Annas and Caiaphas and the rest were of the sons of Aaron, "all who, taking counsel against Jesus, pronounced him guilty of death" and poured out his blood "around the base of the altar of the tabernacle of testimony." For there the blood is poured out where the altar and its base were, as the Lord himself also said: "because it does not befall a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem." He "placed," then, also "his hand upon the head of the calf," that is, he laid the sins of the human race upon his own body; for he himself is the head of the…

"And flaying," it says, "the whole burnt offering, they shall divide it limb by limb, and the sons of Aaron the priest shall put fire upon the altar, and shall pile up wood on the fire; and the sons of Aaron the priest shall lay on the divided limbs and the head and the fat and the wood which are upon the altar. But the entrails and the feet they shall wash with water, and the priest shall lay all upon the altar; it is a victim and a sacrifice, an odor of sweetness to the Lord." How the flesh of the Word of God, which here is named a "calf," is flayed, and how it is divided "limb by limb" by the priests, is worth observing. I think that that priest strips off the hide of the "calf" offered as a "whole burnt offering" and draws off the skin by which its limbs are covered, who strips from the Word of God the veil of the letter and lays bare its inner parts, which are the limbs of…

We strip off the skin of a victim when we remove the illusion of virtue from the eyes of our mind. We cut its limbs into pieces when we carefully distinguish the content of a virtue and ponder it step by step. We should take care, so that when we conquer evil we do not replace it with frivolous goods. Otherwise those goods might produce inconstancy; they might lay hold of frivolity; they might wander off on the path of error; they might be broken by laziness and lose the value of work already done. In all things the mind should look around carefully and persevere in its provident concern. We should also note that we are sometimes afflicted by an impulse to illicit thoughts, because we are engaged in some earthly business, even if it is legitimate. When an earthly act is tinged with desire, even in a small way, the power of the ancient enemy grows against us and our minds are corrupted…

quote: In very many ceremonies of the law one who needed to be cleansed was ordered to be cleansed by [offering] these [birds]. A pigeon indicates simplicity and a turtledove indicates chastity, for a pigeon is a lover of simplicity and a turtledove is a lover of chastity—so that if by chance one loses its mate it will not subsequently seek another.
